inline.s: Stillness Speaks
Eckhart Tolle

A true spiritual teacher does not have anything to teach you in the conventional sense of the word, does not give you anything new in the way of information, belief, or rules of behavior. The only function of a spiritual teacher is to help you remove obstacles. These obstacles separate you from the truth of what you already are, and from what you already know deep within. The spiritual teacher is here to uncover and reveal that deep inner dimension, the dimension of stillness.

If you have come to a spiritual teacher, or to this book, in search of stimulating ideas, theories, beliefs, or intellectual discussion, you will be disappointed. In other words, if you are looking for food for thought, you will not find it. If that is the case, you will miss the essence of this teaching.

The essence of this book is not in the words, but within you. When you listen to this teaching, it will help greatly if you can remember this, and feel this. These words are only signposts. What they point to cannot be found on the level of thought, but on a deeper, vaster level than thought — deep within you.

One of the characteristics of that level is a living stillness, endlessly vibrating. So when you are listening to the teaching, if you sense an inner stillness rising, it means this book is fulfilling its function as your spiritual teacher. It is reminding you of who you are, and pointing directly to the way home.

This is not a book to be read from cover to cover and then put away on the shelf. Live with it; pick it up often. And, more importantly, put it down often; or more often still, hold it without reading it. After reading a short passage, many readers will naturally want to stop, to pause, to reflect on it, and then become still. Every time you stop reading is always more helpful, and more important, than continuing. Allow this book to do its work of awakening you from the ancient jungle — your repetitive, limited thinking.

blocks.text: A Modern Revival of Ancient Spiritual Teachings

inline.s: The form of this book can be seen as a modern revival of the most ancient form of recorded spiritual teaching — the sutras of ancient India. These sutras are powerful pointers to the truth, existing in the form of aphorisms or short phrases, with very little conceptual elaboration. The Vedas and the Upanishads are early teachings on the divine recorded in sutra form, and so are the recorded words of the Buddha. If the sayings and parables of Jesus were extracted from the narrative contexts given them by later writers, they too could be seen as sutras. The profound teachings contained in that ancient Chinese book of wisdom, the Tao Te Ching, likewise exist in sutra form. The virtue of a sutra lies in its brevity and conciseness; it discourages any unnecessary thinking. What it does not say — that to which it merely points — is far more important than what it does say.

In this book, the short sutra-like sentences have been gathered especially in the first chapter, “Silence and Stillness,” which contains only the most concise of them. That chapter holds the essence of the whole book, and for some readers it may be all they need. The other chapters offer more signposts to those who need them. Like the ancient sutras, the sentences in this book are sacred; they come from consciousness, which we may also call stillness. Yet unlike the ancient sutras, they belong to no religious denomination or spiritual tradition, but are teachings immediately accessible to the whole of humanity.

The urgency is greater now, and the transformation of human consciousness is no longer a luxury. It can no longer be, so to speak, something attainable only by a few people who have withdrawn from the world. If humanity is not to destroy itself, this transformation of consciousness is something that must be accomplished. At this very moment, both the dysfunction of the old consciousness and the arising of the new are accelerating. Paradoxically, things are getting worse and better at the same time, although the worse is more noticeable because it makes so much noise.

This book, of course, also becomes thoughts in your mind through the words you read or hear, in the very act of reading or listening. But these are not ordinary thoughts — those repetitive, noisy, self-serving thoughts that clamor for attention. Like every true spiritual teacher, and like the ancient sutras, the thoughts in this book do not say, “Look at me,” but “See through me.”

Because these thoughts come from stillness, they have power, and that power will carry you back to the stillness from which they came. That stillness is also inner peace, and this stillness and peace are your essence. It is this stillness that will save and transform the world.
When you lose touch with inner stillness, you lose touch with yourself. When you lose touch with yourself, you are lost in the world of form.
Your innermost sense of self, of who you are, is inseparable from stillness. This is the “I Am” that is deeper than name and form.

Stillness is your essential nature. What is stillness? It is your inner space or awareness, the inner space in which these words on this page are being read and then become thoughts. Without that awareness there is no perceiving, no thought, no world. You are that awareness, disguised as a person.

The equivalent of external noise is the inner noise of the mind. The equivalent of external silence is inner stillness. Whenever silence surrounds you, listen to it. That means: notice it. Turn your attention toward it. Listening to silence awakens the dimension of stillness within you, for only through stillness can you be aware of silence. Notice this: at the moment you notice the silence around you, you are not thinking. You are conscious, but you are not thinking.
When you become aware of silence, immediately an alert inner stillness arises. You are fully present. You have stepped out of the limitations of thousands of years of human collective conditioning.
Look at a tree, a flower, a plant. Let your awareness rest upon it. They are so still, so deeply rooted in being. Allow nature to teach you stillness.

When you look at a tree and sense its stillness, you become still yourself. You are connected with this tree on a very deep level. Through stillness you feel your oneness with whatever you perceive. To feel your oneness with all things — that is love.

Silence will help, but silence is not always needed in order to find stillness. Even when there is noise, you can sense stillness beneath the noise — the space in which the noise arises. That is pure awareness, the inner space of pure consciousness. You are able to be aware of your own awareness; it is the background of all your perceptions and all your thoughts. To be aware of your awareness means the arising of inner stillness.

Any irritating noise can help us just as much as silence. How? By dropping your inner resistance to the noise and allowing it to be as it is; this acceptance will likewise carry you into inner peace, into stillness. Whenever you accept this moment fully — whatever its outer form — you are still and at peace.

Be aware of the gaps — the gap between two thoughts, the brief silent space between words in a conversation, the pause between the notes of a piano or a flute, or the still point between the in-breath and the out-breath. As you become aware of those gaps, what was awareness of “something” becomes — pure awareness. From within you arises the formless dimension of pure consciousness, and it takes the place of your identification with form.
True intelligence operates silently. In stillness we find creativity and the solution to problems.

Does stillness merely mean the absence of noise or content? No — stillness is intelligence itself; it is the consciousness hidden in the depths, from which every form comes. How could it be separate from you? The outer form you take yourself to be comes from there, and is continually nourished by it. It is the essence of all things, including the galaxies, every blade of grass, flowers, trees, birds, and everything else that has form.
Stillness is the only formless thing in this world. Yet it is not really a thing, nor does it belong to this world.

When you look at a tree or a person in stillness, who is looking? Something deeper than you is looking. It is consciousness looking at its own creation. The Bible says that God created the world and saw that it was good. That is also what you see when you look upon the world from stillness, with no thought in your mind.

Do you need more knowledge? Will richer information save the world? Or faster computers, more scientific or more intelligent analysis? Is it not wisdom, above all, that humanity needs at this moment? But what is wisdom, and where is it to be found? Stillness gives birth to wisdom. Just look, just listen. Nothing else is needed. Remain still, look quietly, listen quietly — it will activate the intelligence within you that is not of the mind. Let stillness direct your words and your actions.
The human condition: lost in thought.
Most people spend their whole lives imprisoned in their own thinking. They never go beyond a narrow, mind-made, prefabricated, label-stamped sense of self conditioned by the past.

As with everyone else, there is within you a dimension of consciousness far deeper than thought. This is your essence. We may call it presence, awareness, the unconditioned consciousness. In the ancient teachings it is called the inner Christ, or your Buddha nature.

When you know only the “small self” manufactured by the mind, and your life is completely in its grip, you create suffering for yourself and others; finding that dimension of presence will liberate you and this world from that suffering. Only through that level of unconditioned consciousness do love, joy, creative expansion, and lasting inner peace come into your life.

If you can recognize that the thoughts passing through your mind are only thoughts, and if you can watch your thinking-emotional reaction patterns as they happen — even only occasionally — this shows that that dimension has begun to take form within you: it is that awareness. Your thinking and your emotions are happening within it; it is the eternal inner space in which the content of your life unfolds.
The stream of thought has tremendous power; it can easily drag you along with it. Every thought pretends to be immensely important. It wants to draw your whole attention to itself.
Here is a new spiritual practice for you: do not take your thoughts so seriously.
How easily people become trapped in the prison of their own concepts!
The human mind is always wanting to know, to understand, to be in control; it always mistakes its own opinions and viewpoints for the truth. The mind always says, “This is how it is.”

You must go beyond your mind. You must realize that however you interpret “your life,” or the lives of others, or their behavior; however you judge a situation — it is nothing more than one viewpoint, one of many possible perspectives. It is nothing more than a bundle of thoughts. But reality is a unified whole in which all things are interconnected and nothing exists on its own. Thinking fragments reality; it cuts the whole into conceptual pieces, one after another.

The thinking mind is a most useful and powerful tool, but it is also very narrow if your life is entirely in its grip, and if you are not aware that the mind is only one small aspect of the infinite consciousness that you truly are.

Wisdom is not a product of thinking. When you give your full attention to a person or a thing, through this simple act a deeper knowing, which is wisdom, arises naturally. Attention is primordial intelligence; it is consciousness itself. It dissolves the barriers created by the mind, and then you will realize that nothing exists on its own. It joins the observer and the observed in the awareness of oneness. It is the healer of separation.
Whenever you are caught in involuntary thinking, you are avoiding what is. You do not want to be present where you are. Here, now.

All dogma — religious, political, scientific — comes from one false belief: that thinking can encompass reality or truth. Dogma is the collective prison of concepts. Strangely, people love their prison cells, because they give a sense of security and a false sense of “I know.”

Nothing has inflicted more suffering on humanity than dogmatism. Every dogma will sooner or later collapse, because reality will eventually expose its error. Yet unless we see through the most fundamental illusion, it will simply be replaced by other dogmas. What is that most fundamental illusion? Identification with thought.
Spiritual awakening is waking up from the dream of thinking.

The realm of consciousness is far vaster than anything thought can grasp. When you no longer identify with what you think, you are freed from thinking, and you realize clearly that the thinker is not you.

The mind is always in a state of “not enough”; it always wants more. When you identify with the mind, you easily become bored and restless. Boredom means that the mind is seeking more stimulation, wanting to bring more food to thinking, and its hunger is not satisfied. When you feel bored, you can satisfy the mind’s hunger in all kinds of ways — pick up a magazine, make a phone call, flick through TV channels, surf the Internet, go shopping — or, and this is not uncommon, transfer the mind’s sense of lack and its need for more onto the body, crudely satisfying it by consuming more things. Or you can abide in the state of boredom and restlessness and observe what boredom and restlessness actually feel like. When you bring awareness to this feeling, suddenly there is some space and stillness around it. At first only a little, but as your inner sense of space keeps growing, the feeling of boredom will begin to become less intense and less important. So even boredom can tell you who you are and who you are not. You discover that “a bored person” is not you. Boredom is nothing but a limited flow of energy within you. Nor are you an angry person, a sad person, or a fearful person. Boredom, anger, sadness, or fear are not “yours”; they are not personal. They are all states of the human mind. They come, and they go. What comes and goes is not you. “I feel bored.” Who is aware of this? “I feel angry, sad, afraid.” Who is aware of this? You are the knowing, not the condition that is known.

Any prejudice means that you have identified with the thinking mind. It means you can no longer see this person, only your opinion of this person. To reduce another person’s living vitality to an opinion is already an act of violence.

Thinking that is not rooted in awareness is self-serving and dysfunctional. Cleverness without wisdom is extremely dangerous and destructive. This is the present condition of most of humanity. Although the increase in technological thinking is in itself neither good nor bad, it has become destructive, because the vast majority of such thinking is not based on awareness. The next step in human evolution is to go beyond thinking. This is our urgent task now. It does not mean never thinking again, but no longer identifying completely with thinking, no longer being controlled by it.

Feel the energy of your inner body. Immediately the noise of your mind slows down or subsides. Feel it in your hands, your feet, your belly, your chest. Feel the life that you truly are, the life that gives vitality to your body. Then your body becomes a gateway; through the body, so to speak, you enter the deep inner aliveness hidden beneath the waves of your emotions and your thinking.

There is an aliveness within you that you can feel with your whole being, not merely in your head. In that presence every cell is alive, and you do not need to think. Only, in that state, if for some practical purpose we need to think, thinking is there. The mind can still function, and it functions beautifully when you are using it through the greater intelligence, when you are expressing that great intelligence itself.

In some brief moments you have already been “thoughtless awareness”; such moments have already happened in your life naturally, instinctively, but you may have overlooked them. Perhaps you were doing handwork, or walking across a room, or waiting at an airline counter, and you were so present that the noisy thoughts of your ordinary mind stopped altogether and were replaced by the presence of awareness. Perhaps you found yourself gazing at the sky, or listening to someone, with no inner commentary in your head at all. Your perception became crystal clear, unobscured by thought. To the mind, such moments are worthless, because there is always something “more important” to think about. They are also utterly unmemorable, which is why you overlook the fact that it is already happening. The truth is that this may be the most important thing that can happen to you. It is the beginning of the shift from thinking into the presence of awareness.

Abide at ease in the state of “not knowing.” This will take you beyond your mind, for the mind always wants to reach conclusions or interpret meanings. It is afraid of the unknown. So when you can abide in not knowing, you have already gone beyond the mind. Out of that state a deeper knowing that is not of the mind arises quietly.

Artistic creation, sports, dance, education, counseling — mastery in any field means that the thinking mind is not involved at all, or at least it is put in second place. A power and intelligence greater than you takes over, and it is also your own essence, which is one with you. There is no longer any process of decision-making; right action arises spontaneously, and “you” are not the doer. To master the art of living means to relinquish control completely. You become attuned to that greater consciousness. It is what acts, speaks, and completes the work.

A crisis moment can temporarily interrupt the stream of thinking and give you a taste of presence, alertness, wakefulness. Truth is all-inclusive; it far exceeds what the mind can comprehend. No thought can encompass truth. At most, thought can point to it. For example, thought can say, “In essence, all things are one.” This is a pointer, not an explanation. To fully realize the meaning of these words means to feel deeply the truth that lives within you, the truth to which these words point.

The mind never stops feeding itself with thinking; more than that, it is constantly seeking identification, seeking a sense of “I.” And so the small self is born, and it endlessly re-creates itself. When you think or talk about yourself, when you say “I,” you usually mean “me and my story.” This “I” is about what you like and dislike, what you fear and desire, and this “I” is never satisfied for long. It is a mind-made sense of who you are, limited by the past, and at the same time forever seeking satisfaction in the future. Do you see that this “I” is fleeting, only a temporary form of existence, like ripples on the surface of water? Who is watching all this? Who is aware of the ever-changing characteristics of your body and your psyche? I am. The deeper “I,” the “I” that has nothing to do with past and future.

Every day, the problem-filled circumstances of your life take up the great majority of your attention and bring you endless fear and desire. Apart from all that, what is left? A little dash — an inch or two long — carved on your tombstone, between your date of birth and your date of death. To the small self, this is a very depressing thought. But to the real you, it is liberation.

When your attention is completely absorbed by thought, it means you have identified with the voice in your head. The thoughts then reinforce the sense of “I.” This is the small self, the “I” manufactured by the mind. This “I” created out of thought always feels deficient and insecure. So fear and lack are the small self’s dominant emotions and driving forces. Once you become aware that there is a voice in your head that always pretends to be you and never stops talking, you awaken from your unconscious identification with the stream of thinking. When you notice that voice, you find that you are not that voice — the thinker — but the one aware of it. To discover that you are the awareness behind the voice is freedom.

The small self is always searching. It keeps searching for this or that to fill itself up, to make itself feel more complete. This explains why the small self is forever involuntarily focused on the future. Whenever you notice that you are “living in the next moment,” you have already stepped out of the small self’s thought patterns, and the possibility arises of choosing to place your full attention on this moment. By giving your full attention to the present, an intelligence far greater than the small self’s mind enters your life.

When you live through the small self, you always downgrade the present moment to a means to an end. You always live in the future, and when you reach your goals, they fail to satisfy you — or at least the satisfaction does not last. When you place more attention on your actions than on the future results you long to achieve through them, you break the old pattern of the small self. Then your actions not only become far more effective, but are filled with boundless satisfaction and joy.

Almost every small self contains at least one element of what we may call a “victim identity.” Some people have such a strong victim self-image that it becomes the core of their small self. Resentment and grievance make up the main part of how they feel about themselves. Even if your grievance is completely “justified,” you have created an identity for yourself that is like a prison, a prison built of the reinforced concrete of your thought patterns. See what you are doing to yourself — or, more precisely, see what your mind is doing to you. Feel the emotion attached to your victim story, be aware of the impulse that always wants to think or talk about that story, and become the witnessing presence of your inner state. You do not need to do anything; with awareness, transformation and freedom come.

Complaining and reacting are the small self’s favorite mental patterns; through them the small self strengthens itself. For many people, a large part of their mental-emotional activity consists of complaining and reacting to this or that. By doing so, you make another person or a situation “wrong” and yourself “right.” By being “right,” you feel superior, and by feeling superior, you reinforce the sense of self. Of course, the truth is that you have only reinforced the illusion of the small self. Can you observe those patterns within you? Can you become aware of the voice in your head that ceaselessly complains about what is?

The sense of the small self always needs conflict, because its sense of separateness is strengthened when it is set against this or that, and reinforced when it shows that this is “me” and that is not “me.” Tribes, nations, and religious denominations often gain a reinforcement of collective identity by having enemies. If there were no “unbelievers,” where would “believers” come from?

When you are with people, can you notice a subtle sense of superiority or inferiority? You are watching the small self, which lives by comparison. Envy is a by-product of the small self: if something good happens to someone else, or someone has more, knows more, or can do more than you, the small self feels diminished. The small self’s identity depends on comparison and feeds on “more.” It will try to grab hold of everything. If all else fails, you can even strengthen your false sense of self by seeing yourself as someone life has cheated, or as sicker than everyone else. What story, what fiction, have you invented to get a sense of self out of it?

To construct this structure of the small self requires opposition, resistance, and exclusion, so that a sense of separateness is maintained; the small self’s survival is built on precisely that sense of separateness. Thus there is an “I” over against “other people,” a “we” over against “them.” The small self needs something or someone to stand against. This is why, although you seek peace, pleasure, and love, you cannot live with them for long. You say you want happiness, yet you are addicted to pain. Fundamentally, your pain does not come from your life circumstances, but from the limitations of your mind.

Do you carry guilt about what you have done in the past — or have not done? One thing is certain: you acted according to the level of your consciousness at the time, or more precisely, the level of your unconsciousness. Had you been more aware, more conscious, you could have acted differently. Guilt is another way the small self tries to create an identity, a sense of “I.” To the small self it does not matter whether that “I” is positive or negative. What you did or did not do was an expression of unconsciousness — humanity’s collective unconsciousness. Yet the small self puts a personal label on it and says, “I did this,” and then you carry around in your mind a “bad” image of yourself. Throughout history, human beings have inflicted countless acts of violence, cruelty, and harm upon one another, and they continue to do so. Should they all be condemned? Are they all guilty? Or are such acts simply expressions of unconsciousness, a stage in human evolution through which we are all growing? Jesus said, “Forgive them, for they know not what they do.” That applies to you as well.

If you set goals for the small self, such as liberating yourself, strengthening yourself, or making yourself feel important, then even if you attain these goals you will not feel fulfilled. Set goals, but understand that what matters is not only attaining them. Whatever arises in presence, it represents the fact that this moment is not a means to an end: the action itself already achieves itself in every moment. You no longer downgrade the present to being a mere means to reach a goal; such thinking belongs to the consciousness of the small self.
“With no self, there is no problem,” was how a great Buddhist master replied when people asked him to explain the deep meaning of the Buddha.

On the surface, it seems that the present moment is just one of very many moments. Each day of your life appears to be composed of tens of thousands of moments in which all kinds of things happen. Yet when you look more deeply, is there not only this one moment? Has life ever existed outside this moment? This moment, the now, is the only place you can never escape. It is the eternal element of your life. No matter what happens. No matter how your life changes. One thing is certain. It is always in the present. Since you cannot escape the present, why not open your arms to it and make friends with it.
When you become friends with this present moment, you will feel at home wherever you are. And when you do not feel at home in the present moment, then wherever you go you will carry unease with you.
The present moment always exists as it is. Can you let it be?

The division of life into past, present, and future is manufactured by the mind, and is essentially illusory. Both past and future are merely modes of thought, abstract concepts in the mind. The past can only be remembered in the present. What you remember is something that once happened at a present moment, and you are also remembering it in the present. The future, when it arrives, is also the present. Therefore the only thing that is real, the only thing that exists, is the present.

Paying attention to the present is not about denying the needs of your life. It means being aware of what is most important. Then you can handle secondary matters with ease. This is not saying: “I will never deal with affairs again, because only the present exists.” No. First discover that which is most important, and make the present your friend rather than your enemy. Face it, respect it. Once the present becomes the foundation and focus of your life, your life will unfold with ease.

Clearing away the dishes, devising a business strategy, planning a trip — what is truly more important: the process of doing, or the result you want to achieve by doing? This moment, or some future moment? Do you look upon this moment as an obstacle to be overcome? Do you feel that you want to reach some future moment, and that it is more important than the present? Almost everyone lives this way most of the time. Since the future never arrives, except as a present moment, this is a dysfunctional way of life. It produces a continual undercurrent of unease, tension, and dissatisfaction. It does not cherish life, and life is the present — there is nothing else besides the present.
Feel the aliveness of your inner body. It can anchor you in the present.

In essence, only when you take responsibility for this present moment are you taking responsibility for life. For the present is the only place where life abides. Taking responsibility for this moment means not resisting the “what is” of the present within, and not arguing with it. It means being in accord with life. The present is as it is because it cannot be otherwise. Now, scientists have verified what Buddhists have always known: nothing and no event exists independently. Beneath the surface phenomena, all things are interrelated; they are all parts of the unity of the universe, and in this present moment the universe brings forth all things. When you say “yes” to what is, you align with the power and the frequency of the intelligence of life itself. Only then can you become a conduit of positive energy that affects this world.
A simple yet highly transformative spiritual practice is this: accept whatever arises in the present — both inner and outer.

When you move your attention into the present, you feel an alertness. It is as if you were waking from a dream, the dream of thinking, the dream of past and future. So clear, so simple. There is no room to create problems. Only this moment as it is.

As you enter the present moment, you realize that life is sacred. When you are present, you discover that everything you perceive is sacred. The more you live in the present, the more you feel the simple and vast joy of “being,” and the sacredness inherent in all things.

Most people confuse the present with what happens in the present, but it is not that. The present is deeper than what happens in it. It is the space that holds them. So do not mix the content of this moment with the present. The present is deeper than any content that occurs within it.

When you enter the present, you step out of the content of the mind. That endless stream of thinking slows down. Thoughts no longer absorb all your attention, no longer drag you away entirely. A gap opens up between thoughts, and space and stillness. You begin to realize that compared with your thoughts, the real you is far vaster and deeper. Thoughts, emotions, perceptions, and everything you experience make up the content of your life. You derive your sense of self from “my life,” and “my life” is satisfying, or so you think. You constantly overlook the most obvious fact: your innermost sense of who you are has nothing to do with what happens in your life, nothing to do with content. That sense of who I am has to do with the present. It is always the same. Whether in childhood or old age, health or illness, success or failure, that I am — the space of the present — at its deepest core always remains unchanged. We often confuse it with content, and as a result you can only faintly, indirectly experience the I am, or the present, through the content of your life. In other words: your sense of “being” is veiled by your surroundings, the stream of your mind, and many other things in this world. The present is veiled by time. So you forget your roots in “being,” your sacred reality, and you lose yourself in this world. When people forget who they are, doubt, anger, depression, violence, and conflict arise. Yet how easy it is to recall the truth, to return home: I am not my thoughts, emotions, perceptions, and experiences. I am not the content of my life. I am life. I am the space where all things happen. I am consciousness. I am the present. I am.

At the deepest level, the present and the real you are inseparable. Many things in your life are urgent, but there is only one thing that is absolutely important. Whether you are successful, or in the eyes of the world a failure, this matters. Whether your body is well or unwell, whether you are learned or unlearned, it matters. Whether you are rich or poor, it matters. It will without doubt bring change to your life. Yes, relatively speaking, all these matters are important. But they are not absolutely important. There is something far more important than any of these, and that is to discover that your essence transcends this transient body, that the real you transcends this transient self-sense that has been labeled as a person. You cannot attain peace by changing the circumstances of your life; you can feel peace only when you realize at the deepest level who you truly are.
If in your next life you still do not know who you are, then even rebirth and reincarnation will not help you.

All the suffering on this planet stems from a sense of “I” or “we” that has been pasted on with labels. It conceals your true essence. When you ultimately remain entirely ignorant of your inner essence, you cannot help but create suffering. It is that simple. When you do not know who you are, you create a mind-made self as a substitute for your beautiful, sacred self, and you cling to this self that is full of fear and greed. You constantly protect and reinforce it, and this erroneous self becomes your primary driving force.

Many everyday expressions, and sometimes even the structure of language itself, reveal the fact that people do not know who they are. You say, “he lost his life,” or “my life,” as if life were something you could possess or lose. The truth is you do not have a life; you are life, this one life, this one consciousness that pervades the whole universe, that experiences itself through transient visible forms — like a stone, a blade of grass, an animal, a person, a star, or an entire galaxy. Can you feel in the depths of your being that you already know it? Can you feel that you already are it?

For most things in life you need time: to learn a new skill, build a house, become an expert, brew a cup of tea. Yet for the most essential thing in life you do not need time. This truly vital matter — self-realization — means realizing that the real you transcends the superficial small self, that it transcends your name, your body, your history, your story. You cannot find yourself in the past or the future. You can only find yourself in the present. Spiritual seekers always seek self-realization or enlightenment in the future. To be a seeker means you need the future. If this is what you think, then it becomes true for you. You will always need time to seek, until you discover that to become the real you requires no time.

When you look at a tree, you are aware of the tree. When you have a thought or a feeling, you are aware of that thought or feeling. When you have a pleasant or painful experience, you are aware of that experience. These all seem to be true and obvious statements. However, if you observe them very carefully, you will discover that within this very structure a basic illusion is subtly contained, and once you use language this illusion is unavoidable. Thought and language create an obvious duality, and a separate person, that do not really exist. The truth of the matter is that you are not the one who is aware of the tree, thought, feeling, or experience. You are that awareness or consciousness in which and through which these things appear. As you live your busy life, can you be aware of yourself as that awareness, within which your whole life content unfolds?

You say: “I want to know myself.” You are the subject, the I. You are the one who knows. You are consciousness itself, through which all things are known, and this consciousness cannot know itself. It is itself. There is nothing beyond it that is known. And all knowing comes from it. The subject I cannot turn itself into an object of knowledge or of consciousness. So you cannot be your own object. This is exactly where the illusion of the small self’s identity arises: in the mind you turn yourself into an object. “This is I,” you say, and then you begin to develop a relationship with yourself, and tell others and yourself a story about you.

By realizing that you are that pure consciousness, and that everything that appears to exist happens within it, you begin to be liberated from your dependence on phenomena, and you no longer seek a self in situations, status, or external conditions. In other words, what has happened or has not happened no longer seems so important. Things are no longer so heavy, so serious. A sense of play comes into your life. You see this world as a cosmic dance, a dance of forms. It is no more and no less than that.

When you know who you truly are, you feel a constant, vibrant stillness. You may call it joy, because joy is precisely this feeling — a living, vibrant stillness. It is the joy of knowing that you are the essence of life, before life takes on the burden of form. It is the joy of being, the joy of being the real you.

Just as water can be solid, liquid, or vapor, consciousness too can appear in different forms. It can be firm as an object, flowing as mind and thought, or formless as pure consciousness. Pure consciousness is precisely the state of life before its manifestation. This life looks upon this world of form through your eyes, because consciousness is you. When you realize you are consciousness, you can recognize yourself in all things. Your perception is so clear. You are no longer the person with a heavy past, which all along had been a screen of concepts that you used to interpret every experience. When you perceive without the interpretation of the mind, you can directly perceive the thing as it truly is. The most fitting words we can find are that, in an alert and still field, perception arises. Through you, formless consciousness becomes aware of itself. Most people’s lives are driven by desire and fear. Desire is wanting to add something to yourself, so as to feel more complete. And all fear is the dread of losing something, lest you be diminished or made smaller. Both kinds of behavior conceal a fact: being cannot be given or taken away. Perfect being is in you, in this present moment.

Whenever you can, look within and see whether you are unconsciously creating conflict between the inner and outer, between the outer environment of that moment — the place you are, the people you are with, what you are doing — and your thoughts and feelings. Can you feel how much you suffer when you resist what is? Once you recognize this, you also realize that you have the freedom to give up this useless struggle and stop the inner state of war.

How many times a day, if you were to put the inner reality of that moment into words, would you have to say, “I do not want to be here”? When you do not want to be here and now — in a traffic jam, at the workplace, in a waiting lounge, with that particular person — what do you feel? Of course, you should indeed leave some places — and sometimes that may be your best choice. But in many cases, leaving is not the way. In these situations, that thought “I do not want to be here” is not only useless but abnormal. It makes both you and those around you unhappy. There is an old saying: where the body is, there the mind is. In other words: you are right here. Always. Is it really so hard to accept this?

Do you really need to label every feeling and experience in your mind? When you are almost constantly in conflict with your surroundings and with people, do you really need to always have a like-or-dislike relationship with life? Or is this just a deep-rooted habit of the mind, a habit that can be broken? Nothing needs to be done; just allow this moment to be as it is.
The habitual reactive “no” reinforces the small self, while “yes” weakens it — your identity of form. This small self cannot survive in surrender.

“I have too much to do.” Yes, but what is the quality of your actions? Driving to work, meeting with clients, working at the computer, running errands, handling the countless trivial matters that make up your life — how engaged are you as you do them? Are you doing them in surrender, or reluctantly? This is where the success of your life is determined, and not by how much effort you expend. Effort implies pressure and tension, needing to reach some point in the future, or to attain some result. Can you detect even the slightest resistance to what you are doing? This is a denial of life, and as a result a truly successful outcome is impossible. If you can be aware of this internally, can you let go of the resistance and throw yourself completely into what you are doing?

“Do one thing at a time.” A Chan master once defined the essence of Chan in this way. Doing one thing at a time means putting your whole being into what you do, with complete attention. This is the action of surrender — action imbued with power.

Your acceptance of what is brings you into a deeper level within; at the same time, your sense of self no longer depends on the mind’s judgments of “good” and “bad.” When you say “yes” to the “what is” of life, when you accept the present moment as it is, you can feel within a great sense of space, and a deep peace. On the surface, you may still feel happy when the weather is fine, and less happy when it rains; you may feel happy when you gain a million dollars, and unhappy when you lose all your property. But these joys and unhappinesses will no longer reach into your depths. They are all only small waves on the surface of your being. Whatever the outer circumstances, your inner peace, which is like a background, can remain undisturbed. This “yes” to what is opens up a deeper dimension within you, one that depends neither on outer circumstances nor on that inner circumstance full of ever-fluctuating thoughts and emotions.

All experience is transient and fleeting, and this world cannot give you anything eternal and unchanging. When you realize this, surrender becomes much easier. Then you continue to relate to people, take part in experiences and activities, but without the greed and fear of the small self. This is to say: you no longer demand that a situation, a person, a place, or a thing should satisfy you or please you. The nature of life as constantly flowing and imperfect is accepted as it is. And the miracle is that when you stop imposing unrealistic demands upon the facts, every situation, every person, every place, or every thing begins to become satisfying, and more harmonious, more peaceful.

When you fully accept the present moment, when you no longer argue with what is, compulsive thinking gradually weakens and is gradually replaced by an alert stillness. You are completely awake, yet the mind no longer labels the present in any way. This inner state of non-resistance carries you into infinite consciousness, which is far greater than the human mind. Then this vast intelligence can express itself through you, and support you both within and without. This is why, by letting go of inner resistance, you will always find that your surroundings become better.
Am I saying: “Enjoy the present moment. Be happy”?
No. Allow the “what is” of the present to exist. That is enough.

Surrender means surrendering to the present moment, not to a story you have fabricated in order to interpret this moment, and which you then try to convince yourself to believe. For example, you may have a disability and can no longer walk. That is the situation. Perhaps your mind is fabricating a story: “My life has come to this. I am ending my days in a wheelchair. Life has been so cruel and unjust to me. I do not deserve this.”
Can you accept the reality of this present moment without mixing it with the story the mind is fabricating around it?
Only when you stop asking, “Why does this happen to me?” does surrender really come.

Even in the situations that seem most unacceptable and most painful, there is hidden a deeper good; in every disaster there is contained a seed of grace. Throughout history, there have been men and women who, when facing great loss, illness, imprisonment, or sudden death, accepted what seemed unacceptable, and so discovered “the peace that surpasses all understanding.” Accepting the unacceptable is the greatest source of grace in this world.

Sometimes all answers and explanations do not work. Life becomes incomprehensible. Or someone in pain comes to you for help, and you do not know what to do or say. When you fully accept that you do not know, you give up using the limited thinking mind to struggle for answers, and it is precisely at this moment that a greater intelligence can work through you. Even thinking itself can benefit from this, because this great intelligence can flow into the mind and inspire it. Sometimes surrender means abandoning the effort to always understand, and becoming comfortable with not knowing.

Do you know someone whose primary function in life seems to be to make themselves and others suffer, spreading unhappiness everywhere? Forgive them, because they too are part of the process of human awakening. The role they play represents an intensification of the nightmare of small-self consciousness, an intensification of the state of non-surrender. None of this has anything to do with the personal. It is not their true nature.

Surrender may be described as an inner transformation, from resistance to acceptance, from “no” to “yes.” When you surrender, your sense of self shifts, from identifying with a reaction or a judgment of the mind, to being the space around this reaction or judgment. This is a shift from identifying with outer form — thought or emotion — to realizing yourself as a formless — vast awareness — existence.
Whatever you fully accept will bring you into stillness, including accepting your non-acceptance, accepting that you are resisting.
Let life be as it is. Let it go with the flow.

We do not only rely on nature for what we need to survive. We also need nature to lead us back onto the road home, out of the prison of our own minds. We are lost in action, thinking, remembering, expecting — lost in a labyrinth of complex things, lost in a world full of problems. What the rocks, the grass, the trees, and the animals still know, we have forgotten. We have forgotten how to be — how to be quiet, how to simply be ourselves, how to dwell in the place where life resides: here and now.

Whenever you notice anything natural, anything that has come into existence without human interference, you step out of the prison of conceptual thinking, and to a certain degree you enter a state of connection with being, the state in which all natural things still abide. To notice a stone, a tree, or an animal does not mean to think about it, but simply to perceive it, letting your consciousness surround it. Then something of its nature is transmitted to you through it. You can feel how still it is, and by doing so the same stillness also rises within you. You feel how deeply it abides in being — completely one with everything happening in the present, one with the place where the present is. By realizing this, you too come to the resting place of the depths within.

When you walk or rest in nature, honor this field with your whole being. Be still. Look. Listen. Every animal and every tree is so at ease. Unlike humans, they have not split themselves in two. They do not live by a self-image in the mind, so they do not need to constantly try to protect or reinforce these images. The elk is itself. The daffodil is itself. All things in nature are not only one with themselves but also one with the whole. They have not separated themselves from the web of the whole, have not declared a separated existence: “I” and a universe other than me. Contemplation of nature can free you from that “I” — that great troublemaker.

Notice the many subtle sounds of nature — the rustling of leaves in the wind, the patter of raindrops falling, the buzzing of insects, the first song of birds at dawn. Give yourself to listening attentively. Beneath these sounds there is something greater: a sacredness that cannot be understood through thinking.

You did not create your body, and you cannot control its functions. A greater intelligence than the human mind is at work. It is this same intelligence that sustains all of nature. Through being aware of your inner energy field — feeling this vitality, this living presence within the body — you no longer have any distance from this intelligence.

A dog’s playfulness and joy, its unconditional love and state of being always ready to celebrate life, often forms a vivid contrast with the inner state of this dog’s owner — depressed, anxious, worried, lost in thinking, always unable to live in the only time and place that truly exists: here and now. One cannot help wondering: how can this dog, living day after day with such a person, still remain so sound, so joyful?

When you perceive nature only through the mind, only through thinking, you cannot feel its vitality, its being. You see only form, and know nothing of the life within the form — that sacred secret. Thought degrades nature into a commodity that can be used in the process of pursuing profit, acquiring knowledge, or pursuing other utilitarian ends. Ancient forests become lumber, a small bird becomes a research project, a mountain becomes something to be mined or conquered. When you perceive nature, make it a space without thought, without mind. When you approach nature in this way, it will respond to you and take part in human evolution and the awakening of planetary consciousness.
Carefully observe how present a flower is, how surrendered to life.

That plant you keep at home — have you ever truly looked at it? Have you ever let this being, at once familiar and mysterious, this thing we call a plant, teach you about its secret? Have you ever noticed how serene it is? Have you ever noticed how it is surrounded by a still field? In the moment you become aware of the stillness and serenity that a plant radiates, it becomes your teacher.

Observe an animal, a flower, a tree, and see how it abides in being. It is itself. It has supreme dignity, purity, and sacredness. Yet to see this you must go beyond the mind’s habit of naming and labeling. In the moment you see through the label of the mind, you feel the ineffable dimension of nature, one that cannot be comprehended by thought nor perceived through the senses. This is a harmony, a sacredness, that not only pervades the whole of nature but also penetrates within you.

The air you breathe is as natural as your breathing process. Pay attention to your breath, and realize that you are not doing it. It is the natural breath. If you had to remember to breathe, you would soon die; if you try to stop breathing, nature will overcome you. Through being aware of your breath, learning to keep your attention on the breath, you reconnect with nature in the most intimate and powerful way. Doing so is deeply healing and gives you great strength. It brings a shift of consciousness, from the conceptual world of thought, into the inner realm of infinite consciousness.

You need nature as a teacher to help you reconnect with being. But it is not only you who need nature; nature needs you too. You are not separate from nature. We are all part of this one life, which manifests throughout the universe as countless visible forms, and every visible form is intimately connected with every other. When, in the place where a flower or a tree stands, you recognize the sacredness, the beauty, the inconceivable stillness and dignity, you give something to that flower or that tree. Through your recognition, your awareness, nature comes to know itself. Through you, it knows its own beauty and sacredness!
A vast, silent space holds the whole of nature in its embrace. It embraces you as well.

Only when there is stillness within you can you enter the field of stillness in which the rocks, the plants, and the animals dwell. Only when your noisy mind subsides can you connect with nature on a deeper level and go beyond the sense of separation that excessive thinking creates. Thinking is a stage in the evolution of life. Before thought appeared, nature existed in pure stillness. Trees, flowers, birds, and rocks are utterly unaware of their beauty and their sacredness. When human beings become still, they go beyond thought. In the stillness that transcends thought, a dimension of knowing is added, a dimension of awareness. Nature can bring you into stillness. This is its gift to you. When you perceive the field of stillness of nature and enter into it, that field of stillness is pervaded by your awareness. This is your gift to nature. Through you, nature begins to know itself. Nature has always been waiting for you; as in the past, it has waited for you for millions of years.

We form an opinion about a person, and reach a verdict on them, so very quickly. To label another person, to give them a conceptual identity, or to pronounce a just judgment upon them — all of this always satisfies the mind of the small self. Everyone’s way of thinking and behaving is conditioned to some degree — limited by their genes, their childhood experiences, and their cultural environment. This is not their essence; it is only how they appear. When you pass a moral judgment on someone, you confuse their conditioned mind with who they truly are. Doing so is itself a deeply limited, unconscious pattern. You impose a conceptual identity on them, and that false identity becomes a prison that confines them and confines you as well. To let go of judgment does not mean that you no longer see what they do. It means that you see their behavior as a conditioned outward form, and you see it and accept it as it is. You do not construct an identity for that person. This frees both you and that person from identification with conditions, with outward form, with the mind. The small self no longer controls your relationships.

As long as the small self is in charge of your life, most of your thoughts, emotions, and actions come from desire and fear. In relationships, then, you are either wanting something from the other person or fearing something in them. What you want from them may be happiness, or material gratification, or recognition, appreciation, attention, or else a strengthening of your sense of self through comparison — through making sure that you know more than they do and possess more than they do. And what you fear is that the opposite may be the case: you fear that in some way they may diminish your sense of self. When you focus your attention on the present moment — instead of seeing the present as a means to an end — you go beyond the small self, beyond the unconscious compulsion to use others in order to reach your goals and to sacrifice them in order to strengthen yourself. When you give your full attention to anyone you interact with, you leave past and future outside the relationship, except when you need to deal with practical matters. When you interact in full presence with everyone you meet, you let go of the definition you once imposed on them — your interpretation of who they are and what they have done — and you can interact with them free of any desire or fear of the small self. Attention, which is alert stillness, is the key. What a wonderful thing it is to be able to go beyond desire and fear in your relationships. Love needs nothing and fears nothing.

If her past were your past, her pain your pain, her level of consciousness your level of consciousness, you would think and act exactly as she does. Realize this, and forgiveness, compassion, and peace follow. The small self does not like to hear this, for once it can no longer react and is no longer right, it loses its power.
When you receive anyone who enters the space of the present moment as your honored guest, when you allow each person to be as they are, they begin to change.

If you want to know a person in their essence, you do not really need to know anything about them — their past, their history, their story. We constantly confuse knowing about with a deeper kind of knowing, the non-conceptual knowing. Knowing about and knowing are entirely different forms. One has to do with outward form, the other with the formless. One operates through thinking, the other through stillness. Knowing about is useful for practical purposes. On that level we cannot do without it. Yet if it becomes the prevailing form in a relationship, it turns very limiting, even destructive. Thinking and concepts create an artificial barrier, a sense of separation between people. Your interaction is then not rooted in being but based in the mind. Without the barrier of concepts, love flows naturally in the interaction between people.

Most people’s interactions are confined to an exchange of words — the realm of thinking. What matters is to bring some stillness into your interactions, especially into your intimate relationships. Without the sense of vast space that comes from stillness, no relationship can develop in a healthy way. Meditate together, or sit quietly together in nature for a while. When you go for a walk together, or sit in a car, or are at home, learn to be at ease and at peace in being still together. Stillness cannot be created, nor does it need to be. It is already there; it is only often obscured by the noise of the mind. All that is needed is to be open to it and feel it. Once the vast stillness is lost, the relationship is taken over by the mind and is easily taken captive by problems and conflict. If stillness is there, it can contain everything.

True listening is another way of bringing stillness into a relationship. When you truly listen to someone, a dimension of stillness arises and becomes a vital part of that relationship. But true listening is a very rare skill. Usually, most of a person’s attention is occupied by their own thinking. At best, they may be evaluating your words, or preparing the next thing they are going to say. They may not be listening at all, but simply lost in their own thoughts. True listening goes far deeper than the perception of hearing. It is the arising of alert attention, a space of presence in which the words are received. The words now become secondary. They may make sense, or they may make no sense at all. Far more important than what you are listening to is the act of listening itself, the space of conscious presence that arises as you listen. That space is a unified field of awareness in which you meet another human being, without the separating barrier created by conceptual thinking. The other person is then no longer “other.” In that space you merge with one another and become one awareness, one consciousness.

Have you ever experienced a drama that keeps repeating itself in your intimate relationships? Do relatively unimportant little disagreements often trigger fierce arguments and emotional pain? Deep within all this lies the basic pattern of the small self: it has to be right, and then of course the other person has to be wrong — in other words, identification with the mind’s position. The small self also needs to be in conflict with something or someone from time to time, in order to strengthen the sense of separation between me and others; without that sense of separation, the small self cannot survive. In addition, you and every human being carry within you an accumulation of emotional pain, coming from your personal past and also from the collective pain of humanity, a pain that reaches back very, very far. This pain-body is an energy field within you that takes you over from time to time, because it needs to keep experiencing emotional pain in order to feed and replenish itself. It will try to take charge of your thinking and make your thoughts extremely negative. The pain-body loves your negative thoughts, because it can resonate with every frequency of those thoughts and so feed on them. It will also provoke negative emotional reactions in those around you, especially your partner, so that it can feed on the drama and emotional pain that follow. This unconscious identification with pain creates so much unhappiness in life — how can you free yourself from it? Become aware of the pain. Realize that it is not who you truly are; recognize it for what it is — nothing but past pain. When it arises in your partner or in yourself, watch it. When you break your unconscious identification with it, you are able to observe it within yourself; you no longer feed it, and gradually it loses its supply of energy. Human interaction can be hell. Or it can become a great spiritual practice.

When you look at another person and a great love rises in you, or when you gaze at the beauty of nature and feel a deep response within, close your eyes for a moment and sense the essence of that love or beauty within you, which is inseparable from who you truly are, inseparable from your own true nature. Outward form is only a fleeting reflection of your inner essence. And so all outward forms will pass away, while love and beauty will never leave you.

What is your relationship to this material world, to the countless things that surround you and that you deal with every day? This chair you are sitting on, this pen, this car, this cup. Are they for you merely tools to an end? Or do you sometimes become aware of their existence, their being, however brief the moment — you notice them, you give them your attention. When you are attached to material things, when you use them to raise your value in your own eyes and in the eyes of others, your attention to things can easily take over your entire life. When you derive your sense of self from things, you no longer appreciate them as they are, because you are looking for yourself in them. When you appreciate an object as it is, when you recognize its being without any projection of the mind, gratitude for its existence will surely arise in you. You may even sense that it is not truly inanimate, that it merely appears lifeless to our senses. Physicists would confirm this: at the molecular level, it is indeed a vibrating energy field. By appreciating things from the perspective of no-self, the world around you begins to come alive in ways your mind cannot comprehend. Whenever you meet a person, however brief the time, do you give them your full attention and so recognize their being — or do you reduce them to a tool to an end, a lowly function or role? What is the quality of your relationship with the supermarket cashier, the parking lot attendant, the repairman, the customer? A moment of attention is enough. As you look at them or listen to them, an alert stillness arises. Perhaps only for two or three seconds. Perhaps a little longer. That brief moment is enough for something to come into being that is more real than the roles we usually play or identify with. All roles are part of the conditioned consciousness of the human mind. What comes into being through attention, however, is the unconditioned — your true essence beneath your name and outward form. You no longer act according to a script. You become real. When that dimension rises from within you, it also draws forth that dimension in others. Of course, in the end there is no other; you always meet yourself.

When you walk through a forest that has not yet been cleared and disturbed by people, you see not only the rich and varied life around you but also fallen trees, dead wood, and, with every step, decaying leaves and decomposing matter underfoot. Wherever you look, you see death and life at the same time. Yet if you look closely, you will find that the decomposing trunk and the rotting branches and leaves not only give birth to new life — they are themselves full of life. Microorganisms are at work. Molecules are rearranging themselves. So death is nowhere to be found. There is only the ever-evolving form of life. Can you learn something from this? Death is not the opposite of life. Life has no opposite. The opposite of death is birth. And life is eternal.

Since ancient times, sages and poets have acknowledged the dreamlike nature of human existence — it seems so solid and so real, yet it is so brief and fleeting, at any moment liable to dissolve into nothing. At the moment of approaching death, your life story may indeed seem like a dream that is about to end. Yet even in a dream there must be something real and true. There must be a consciousness in which the dream happens; otherwise the dream could not exist. That consciousness — was it created by this body, or did consciousness create this dream of a body, this dream of a someone? Why is it that most people who have had a near-death experience are no longer afraid of death? Think about it carefully.

Of course, you know that one day you will die, but that is only a concept in the mind until you face death “in person” for the first time: perhaps you or someone close to you falls gravely ill, or has an accident; perhaps someone you love passes away, and death enters your life, and you realize that you too cannot escape it. In the face of death, most people choose to flee out of fear. But if you choose not to retreat, if you bravely face the fact that your body is brief and fleeting, at any moment liable to dissolve into nothing, you are freed to some degree from identification with this body-and-mind structure, with this “me.” When you understand and accept the impermanent nature of all life forms, an unusual sense of peace descends upon you. By facing death, your consciousness is to some degree freed from identification with outward form. This is why, in some Buddhist traditions, monks visit the charnel grounds regularly and sit in meditation among corpses. In Western culture, the denial of death is still widespread. Even old people try not to discuss or think about death; corpses are hidden away. A culture that denies death will without doubt be shallow and superficial, concerned only with outward appearances. Once death is denied, life loses its depth. We lose the opportunity to know that we truly are beyond name and form, and to know that transcendent dimension; that possibility disappears from our lives, because death is precisely the door into that dimension.

People are always ill at ease with endings of every kind, for every ending is a little death. This is why in many different languages the word for goodbye means “we will see each other again.” Whenever an experience is about to end — a gathering of friends, a holiday, your children leaving home — you die a little. An outward form that once appeared in your consciousness as this experience dissolves. This often leaves a feeling of emptiness, which most people do their utmost not to feel, not to face. If you can learn to accept, even to welcome, these endings in your life, you may find that the emptiness that at first made you uneasy transforms into a sense of vast inner space, bringing you deep peace. By learning to die in this way each day, you open yourself to life.

Most people feel that their identity, their sense of self, is something so precious that they do not want to lose it. This is why they are so afraid of death. That “I” will one day cease to exist — this sounds simply unimaginable and fills them with dread. But you have confused the truly precious “I” with your name, your form, and the story associated with them. That “I” is merely a fleeting form within the field of consciousness. If all you know is this form identity, you still do not understand that what is truly precious is your essence, the deepest “I am” within you — consciousness itself. It is the eternal within you — the only thing you cannot possibly lose.

Whenever a major loss occurs in your life — the loss of property, of a home, of an intimate relationship; or the loss of reputation, work, or your capacity to work — something within you dies. You feel diminished. You may also feel a kind of bewilderment. “Without these … who am I?”

When some outward form leaves you or dissolves, and you have unconsciously identified with it as part of yourself, this can bring immense pain. It is, so to speak, like leaving a hole in the structure of your being. When this happens, do not deny or ignore the pain or grief you feel. Accept that they are there. Your mind always tends to weave a story around this loss, a story in which it assigns you the role of victim; be aware of this trick of the mind. Fear, anger, resentment, or self-pity are the emotions that come with that role.

Next, become aware of what lies behind these emotions and the stories the mind fabricates: the hole, the space. Can you face and accept this unfamiliar sense of emptiness? If you can, you may find that it is no longer frightening. You may be surprised to discover the stillness and peace that radiate from this emptiness. Whenever death occurs, whenever a life form dissolves, God — the formless, the unmanifested — shines through the open space left by the dissolved form. This is why the most sacred thing in life is death. This is why, through contemplating and accepting death, the peace of God descends upon you.

Everyone’s journey is so brief; life passes in a flash. Is there anything that is not subject to birth and death? Is there anything eternal? Consider this: if there were only one color, blue, and the whole world and everything in it were blue, then blue would not exist. There must be something that is not blue for blue to be recognized; otherwise blue could not “stand out,” could not exist. By the same reasoning, must there not also be something that is not brief, not fleeting, for the impermanence of all things to be recognized? In other words: if everything, including you, were not enduring, could you even recognize that? Does the very fact that you can be aware of and witness the fleeting nature of all things, including yourself, not mean that there is something within you that never fades? When you were twenty, you were aware that your body was strong and full of vitality; sixty years later, you are aware that your body is weak and aging. Since you were twenty, your thoughts may have changed a great deal, but the awareness that knows your body to be young or old, the awareness that knows your thoughts have changed, has never changed. That awareness is the eternal within you — it is consciousness itself. It is the formless, unified life. Will you lose it? No, because you are it.

Some people become very peaceful, almost luminous, before they die, as if something were shining through the dissolving body. It may be said that sometimes those who are gravely ill, or the very old, become almost transparent in the last weeks, months, or even years of their lives. When they look at you, you may see a light radiating from their eyes. There is no more psychological suffering. They have surrendered, and so the person, the mind-made small self, has dissolved. They have “died before death”; they have discovered the peace at the depth of their being and realized the eternal, deathless essence within them.

In every accident and disaster there lies a hidden redemption of which we are usually unaware. The tremendous shock of a sudden death can force your consciousness completely out of identification with form. In the final moments of the body’s death, and at the moment of death itself, you experience yourself as formless consciousness. Suddenly there is no more fear, only stillness; you know that “all is well,” and that death is merely the dissolution of an outward form. Then you realize that death is, after all, illusory — as illusory as the body you once identified as yourself. Death is not, as modern culture would have you believe, an anomaly, or the most terrible of all events; it is the most natural thing in the world, as natural as the birth that corresponds to it. Death and life are inseparable. Remember this when you sit beside someone who is about to die. To be present as you witness and accompany a person’s death is a great honor and a sacred act. When you sit beside a dying person, do not deny any aspect of this experience. Do not deny what is happening, and do not deny what you feel. Discovering that there is nothing you can do may make you feel helpless, sad, or angry. Accept your feelings. Then go one step deeper: accept that at this moment you can do nothing — accept this completely. You are not in control of any of it. Surrender deeply to every aspect of this experience, surrender to your feelings, surrender to the pain or discomfort the dying person may be experiencing. The surrendered state of your consciousness and the stillness that accompanies it will be of immense help to the dying person and will make the process of transition easier. If you feel like speaking, the words will come from the stillness within you. But words are secondary. What comes with that stillness is a deep blessing: peace.

blocks.text: Chapter 10: Suffering and the End of Suffering

inline.s: All things are interconnected: Buddhists have long known this, and physicists now confirm it. Nothing happens in isolation, though it may appear to. The more we judge and label, the more we isolate. Because of our thinking, the oneness of life falls into fragments. Yet this very event is brought about by the totality of life. It is part of this web of connectedness, of the cosmic order. This means that whatever is happening in the present moment is what is, and it cannot be otherwise. For the most part, we cannot begin to understand what role an apparently meaningless event may play in the cosmic order as a whole. But if we have some sense of the inevitability of this event within the vast and boundless whole, an inner acceptance of the “what is” of the present moment opens up, and we begin to be in harmony with the totality of life.

To live in this way is true freedom and the end of suffering: whatever you feel or experience in this moment, see it entirely as your own choice. To be in inner harmony with the present moment is the end of suffering.

Is suffering really necessary? Yes and no. If you had not suffered as you have, you would have no depth as a human being — no humility, no compassion. You would not be listening to this teaching now. The wounds of suffering have cracked open the shell of the small self. Then suffering has fulfilled its purpose. Suffering is necessary until you realize that it is unnecessary.

An unpleasant feeling needs a mind-made “me” and a story; it needs this conceptual identity. It also needs time, past and future. When you remove time from your unhappiness, what is left? This moment as it is, here and now. In that moment you may feel heavy, anxious, tense, angry, even nauseated. This is not unhappiness, and it is not a personal problem. Nothing in human suffering is personal. It is simply a great pressure or energy that you feel somewhere in the body. By giving it your attention, this feeling does not turn into thinking, nor does it activate the unhappy me. If you simply allow a feeling to be, see what happens.

If you take every thought that enters your mind seriously, it gives rise to a great deal of pain and unhappiness. Situations do not make you unhappy. They may bring physical pain, but they do not make you unhappy. It is your thoughts that make you unhappy. Your interpretation, the story you tell yourself, is what makes you unhappy. “It is some of my thoughts at this moment that are making me unhappy.” This realization breaks your unconscious identification with those thoughts.

“What a miserable day.” “He didn’t call me back, how rude.” “She let me down so badly.” Usually we tell ourselves and others these little stories in the form of complaints. We unconsciously design these complaints to strengthen our impoverished sense of self by making ourselves right and other people or circumstances wrong. “I am right” places us in an imagined sense of superiority and so reinforces this false self, this small self. It also creates an enemy. Yes, the small self needs an enemy to define its boundaries. Even the weather can serve that function. Through habitual mental judgment and emotional contraction, you have a personalized reactive pattern toward the people and things in your life. These are all self-made forms of suffering, but people are not aware of them, because they satisfy the small self. Through habitual reaction and conflict, the small self strengthens itself. How simple life would be without those stories. “It is raining.” “He didn’t call back.” “I went, she didn’t.”
When you are suffering, when you are unhappy, be fully with that moment. Neither unhappiness nor trouble can survive in the present.

Suffering begins when you mentally name or label a situation as annoying or bad. You resent a situation, and this resistance personalizes it and brings in the reactive me. Naming and labeling are habitual, but the habit can be broken. Begin to practice not naming with small things. If you miss your flight, break a cup, or slip in the mud, can you hold yourself back from labeling the experience as bad or painful? Can you immediately accept this moment as it is? Labeling something as bad triggers an emotional contraction in your body; when you do not label it but simply let it be, suddenly you feel a great power. That contraction cuts you off from this power, the power of life itself.

They ate the fruit of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. Hold yourself back from constantly labeling things in your mind as good or bad, and you go beyond the duality of good and evil. When you go beyond the habit of naming, the power of the universe flows through you. When you no longer react habitually to an experience, the experiences you once called bad are transformed by the power of life itself; even if the change is not immediate, it often comes fairly soon. When you no longer name an experience as bad but instead give it an inner acceptance, an inner “yes,” and allow it to be, see what happens.
Whatever your life situation, if, right now, you completely accepted it as it is, how would you feel?

Suffering has many different forms, subtle or not so subtle, and they are so commonplace that people often do not regard them as suffering; they may even satisfy the small self. Aversion, fretfulness, rage, displeasure with something or someone, hatred, complaining. When they occur, you can learn to recognize these forms of suffering and realize that in this moment I am creating suffering for myself. If you are habitually creating suffering for yourself, you are very likely also causing suffering for others. Simply recognize them when they occur and make them conscious, and the unconscious chatter of the mind will gradually subside. You cannot be conscious and at the same time be creating suffering for yourself.

This is the miracle. Behind every apparently “bad” or “evil” event, person, or situation, there lies a deeper “good.” Through your inner acceptance of what is in this present moment, this deeper “good” reveals itself to you from within. “Do not resist evil” is one of the highest truths of humanity.
A dialogue:
“Accept the situation as it is.”
“I really can’t do it. I feel agitated and angry about this.”
“Then accept your present condition.”
“Accept that I feel agitated and angry now? Accept my inability to accept?”
“Yes. Bring acceptance into your non-acceptance. Bring surrender into your non-surrender. Then see what happens.”

Chronic physical pain is one of the strictest teachers you can encounter. What it teaches you is this: resistance is futile. Nothing is more common than the “unwillingness to suffer.” Yet, if you can set aside this unwillingness and allow the pain to be there, you may notice that you separate subtly from the pain, that a gap opens between you and it, and that this gap has always existed. This means suffering consciously and willingly. When you suffer consciously, physical pain can quickly burn up your ego, because the ego is to a great extent composed of resistance. This is also true of severe physical disability. To “offer your pain to God” is another way of speaking this truth. You do not have to be a Christian to grasp the profound cosmic truth contained in the symbol of the cross. The cross is an instrument of torture. It represents the greatest pain, limitation, and helplessness that a person can encounter. Then, suddenly, that person bears the pain willingly, with full awareness, expressing it through these words: “Not my will, but thy will be done.” In that moment the cross, the instrument of torture, reveals its hidden face. At once it is a sacred symbol, a symbol of the divine. The cross, which seems to deny that any transcendent dimension exists in life, becomes, through surrender, the gateway to that dimension.
